query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for jet-turbine applications, what single intervention could improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its mechanism, the expected improvement relative to a relevant baseline, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive experiment with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled post‐processing aging treatment that induces a uniform dispersion of coherent, nanoscale strengthening precipitates (for example, an L1₍₂₎-type phase) within a low‐density refractory HEA matrix will boost high‑temperature yield strength and creep resistance without increasing alloy density or detrimentally affecting room‑temperature ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: A low‑density refractory high‑entropy alloy (e.g. one where heavier refractory elements are partially substituted with lighter ones such as Ti or Al) having a homogeneous single‑phase body‑centered cubic (BCC) solid solution structure.
generation.intervention: Application of an optimized aging heat treatment designed to promote the nucleation and growth of coherent, nanoscale L1₍₂₎ precipitates in the BCC matrix.
generation.conditions: Performance evaluated under service‐relevant high temperatures (e.g., up to ≈900°C as in jet‐turbine environments) under tensile/creep loading, while also maintaining mechanical performance at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a uniformly dispersed, coherent nanoprecipitate phase (L1₍₂₎) that remains finely scaled and stable at elevated temperatures.
generation.mechanism: The coherent nanoprecipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion, thereby enhancing high‑temperature yield strength and creep resistance via precipitation strengthening without compromising the ductile, low‑density BCC matrix that dominates mechanical behavior at room temperature.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as‑cast or solution‑treated baseline, the aged alloy should exhibit a marked improvement in high‑temperature mechanical properties (e.g. higher yield strength and longer creep rupture life) while showing similar density and adequate room‑temperature ductility.
generation.baseline: The same low‑density refractory HEA in the as‑cast/solution‑treated condition without any aging treatment to induce controlled, nanoscale precipitates.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only if the aging treatment is precisely controlled; if precipitates coarsen (over-aged condition) or form brittle intermetallic phases beyond the optimal volume fraction, room‑temperature performance or ductility could degrade.
generation.uncertainty: Ideal aging parameters (temperature, time) for achieving the optimal precipitate size and volume fraction are not yet known, and the interplay with any competing secondary phases may introduce variability that requires further experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of identical low‑density refractory HEA samples. Subject one group to the proposed aging heat treatment (with parameters chosen to favor coherent L1₍₂₎ precipitate formation) and keep the second group as an untreated control. Evaluate both groups using microstructural characterization (TEM/SEM) as well as mechanical tests at room temperature and at high temperatures up to 900°C under tensile and creep load conditions.
measurements: TEM/SEM analysis to measure precipitate size, distribution, and coherence
Room‑temperature tensile tests (to assess ductility and yield strength)
High‑temperature tensile and creep tests (to measure yield strength and creep rupture life)
Density measurement to confirm no significant increase
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aging treatment does not lead to a statistically significant improvement (e.g., increased high‑temperature strength or extended creep life) compared to the control, or if it results in a reduction of room‑temperature ductility or an increase in density, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

Abstract High entropy or compositionally complex alloys provide opportunities for optimization towards new high-temperature materials. Improvements in the equiatomic alloy Al 17 Co 17 Cr 17 Cu 17 Fe 17 Ni 17 (at.%) led to the base alloy for this work with the chemical composition Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (at.%). Characterization of the beneficial particle-strengthened microstructure by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and observation of good mechanical properties at elevated temperatures arose the need of accomplishing further optimization steps. For this purpose, the refractory metals hafnium and molybdenum were added in small amounts (0.5 and 1.0 at.% respectively) because of their well-known positive effects on mechanical properties of Ni-based superalloys. By correlation of microstructural examinations using SEM with tensile tests in the temperature range of room temperature up to 900 °C, conclusions could be drawn for further optimization steps. Keywords: HEA, high entropy alloys, compositionally complex alloys, mechanical characterization
